title: Understanding Digital Signal Processing, 3rd Edition
topics: Front matter (PDF pp. 1-25): preface, intended audience, third-edition changes, acknowledgments, notation, and contents for the assigned material.
1.1 Discrete Sequences and Systems (PDF p. 26): sampled sequences, sample indices, amplitude, and the fact that a discrete sequence has no defined values between samples.
1.2 Signal Amplitude, Magnitude, Power (PDF p. 32): signed amplitude, nonnegative magnitude, and power proportional to squared amplitude.
1.3 Signal Processing Operational Symbols (PDF p. 33): adders, multipliers, and unit delays as the primitives of DSP block diagrams.
1.4 Introduction to Discrete Linear Time-Invariant Systems (PDF p. 35): linearity, additivity, homogeneity, and time invariance.
1.5 Discrete Linear Systems (PDF p. 35): linear-system tests and the spectral consequences of nonlinear operations.
1.6 Time-Invariant Systems (PDF p. 40): shift-equivalence test for time invariance.
1.7 The Commutative Property of Linear Time-Invariant Systems (PDF p. 41): interchangeable order of cascaded LTI systems.
1.8 Analyzing Linear Time-Invariant Systems (PDF p. 42): impulse response, convolution, and frequency response.
Chapter 1 problems (PDF pp. 44-51): 24 short exercises on sequence notation, block diagrams, linearity, time invariance, and impulse response.
2.1 Aliasing: Signal Ambiguity in the Frequency Domain (PDF p. 52): indistinguishable sampled sinusoids and spectral replicas.
2.2 Sampling Lowpass Signals (PDF p. 56): Nyquist criterion, spectral folding, and analog anti-alias filtering.
2.3 Sampling Bandpass Signals (PDF p. 59): valid undersampling regions for a band-limited passband signal.
2.4 Spectral Inversion in Bandpass Sampling (PDF p. 63): inversion under odd-order folding and reinversion with multiplication by (-1)^n.
Chapter 2 problems (PDF pp. 66-73): 22 numerical and graphical exercises on lowpass and bandpass sampling, aliases, inversion, and noise folding.
3.1 Understanding the DFT Equation (PDF p. 75): DFT as correlation with N complex sinusoids and bin spacing fs/N.
3.2 DFT Symmetry (PDF p. 86): conjugate symmetry for real sequences and symmetry consequences of real-even and real-odd inputs.
3.3 DFT Linearity (PDF p. 87): transform of a weighted sum.
3.4 DFT Magnitudes (PDF p. 88): scaling of DC, real sinusoids, and complex sinusoids.
3.5 DFT Frequency Axis (PDF p. 89): bin-to-frequency mapping and interpretation of negative-frequency bins.
3.6 DFT Shifting Theorem (PDF p. 89): time shifts as linear phase ramps with invariant magnitude.
3.7 Inverse DFT (PDF p. 91): synthesis equation and its sign and scale differences from the forward DFT.
3.8 DFT Leakage (PDF p. 92): endpoint discontinuity, nonintegral cycles, and the sinc/Dirichlet spreading of energy across bins.
3.9 Windows (PDF p. 99): leakage suppression versus main-lobe widening for rectangular, triangular, Hanning/Hann, Hamming, Blackman, Chebyshev, and Kaiser windows.
3.10 DFT Scalloping Loss (PDF p. 106): amplitude error for tones between DFT bin centers.
3.11 DFT Resolution, Zero Padding, and Frequency-Domain Sampling (PDF p. 107): distinguish display interpolation from true frequency resolution.
3.12 DFT Processing Gain (PDF p. 110): concentration of coherent tones relative to broadband noise.
3.13 The DFT of Rectangular Functions (PDF p. 113): Dirichlet-kernel transform and reciprocal time/frequency widths.
3.14 Interpreting the DFT Using the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (PDF p. 125): DTFT continuity and periodicity, DFT samples, and periodic extension.
Chapter 3 problems (PDF pp. 129-137): 25 exercises spanning hand DFTs, symmetry, leakage, windows, zero padding, gain, and rectangular sequences.
4.1 Relationship of the FFT to the DFT (PDF p. 138): FFT as an exact efficient DFT and radix-2 length requirements.
4.2 Hints on Using FFTs in Practice (PDF p. 140): sampling ratio, record duration, mean removal, windowing order, scaling, averaging, and real-input opportunities.
4.3 Derivation of the Radix-2 FFT Algorithm (PDF p. 143): even/odd decimation and recursive butterfly construction.
4.4 FFT Input/Output Data Index Bit Reversal (PDF p. 150): binary index reversal and data ordering.
4.5 Radix-2 FFT Butterfly Structures (PDF p. 151): equivalent butterfly flowgraphs and optimized complex arithmetic.
4.6 Alternate Single-Butterfly Structures (PDF p. 154): in-place versus double-memory architectures and twiddle-factor storage.
Chapter 4 problems (PDF pp. 158-166): 18 exercises on FFT operation counts, indexing, butterflies, ordering, and implementation.
5.1 An Introduction to Finite Impulse Response Filters (PDF p. 168): moving-average intuition, tapped-delay-line convolution, and finite impulse response.
5.2 Convolution in FIR Filters (PDF p. 171): coefficient/impulse-response identity and convolution as filtering.
5.3 Lowpass FIR Filter Design (PDF p. 181): ideal frequency samples, inverse transform to sinc-like coefficients, truncation, and Gibbs ripple.
5.4 Bandpass FIR Filter Design (PDF p. 195): modulating a lowpass impulse response to shift its passband.
5.5 Highpass FIR Filter Design (PDF p. 196): spectral translation via alternating coefficient signs.
5.6 Parks-McClellan Exchange FIR Filter Design Method (PDF p. 197): optimal equiripple/Chebyshev approximation.
5.7 Half-band FIR Filters (PDF p. 200): alternating zero coefficients, symmetry about fs/4, and reduced computation.
5.8 Phase Response of FIR Filters (PDF p. 201): linear phase, phase delay, group delay, and symmetric/antisymmetric coefficients.
5.9 A Generic Description of Discrete Convolution (PDF p. 206): flip-and-slide convolution and output length P+Q-1.
5.10 Analyzing FIR Filters (PDF p. 216): frequency response from coefficients, magnitude/phase/group delay, DC gain, and tap estimates.
Chapter 5 problems (PDF pp. 225-236): 29 design and analysis exercises on convolution, windowed FIRs, modulation, half-band structure, and phase.
6.1 An Introduction to Infinite Impulse Response Filters (PDF p. 238): output feedback, recursive difference equations, and IIR efficiency/phase tradeoffs.
6.2 The Laplace Transform (PDF p. 240): continuous-system transfer functions, poles, zeros, impulse responses, frequency response, and s-plane stability.
6.3 The z-Transform (PDF p. 251): discrete-time transfer functions, unit-circle frequency contour, poles, zeros, and z-plane stability.
6.4 Using the z-Transform to Analyze IIR Filters (PDF p. 254): z^-1 as delay, Direct Form I, H(z), H(omega), and a complete second-order example.
6.5 Using Poles and Zeros to Analyze IIR Filters (PDF p. 262): factored and polynomial transfer functions and geometry-based response inference.
6.6 Alternate IIR Filter Structures (PDF p. 267): Direct Forms I/II, transposed structures, the transposition theorem, and finite-precision differences.
6.7 Pitfalls in Building IIR Filters (PDF p. 270): coefficient quantization, overflow, roundoff, limit cycles, deadband, dither, saturation, and word width.
6.8 Improving IIR Filters with Cascaded Structures (PDF p. 272): cascade/parallel identities, ripple estimates, and biquad section pairing/order.
6.9 Scaling the Gain of IIR Filters (PDF p. 276): DC/passband normalization and internal dynamic-range scaling.
6.10 Impulse Invariance IIR Filter Design Method (PDF p. 278): sampled analog impulse responses, aliasing, two derivations, and a Chebyshev example.
6.11 Bilinear Transform IIR Filter Design Method (PDF p. 292): stable s-to-z mapping, frequency warping, prewarping, and worked design.
6.12 Optimized IIR Filter Design Method (PDF p. 302): iterative coefficient fitting to arbitrary desired responses.
6.13 A Brief Comparison of IIR and FIR Filters (PDF p. 303): linear phase, analog-prototype emulation, multiply counts, data rate, and measured execution speed.
Chapter 6 problems (PDF pp. 306-327): 50 exercises on transforms, poles/zeros, structures, quantization, cascade/scaling, and IIR design.
key_results: Sec. 1.1 (PDF pp. 26-32): a discrete sequence is defined only at integer sample indices; absolute frequency requires the sample period or sample rate, not merely the plotted sample pattern.

Secs. 1.4-1.6 (PDF pp. 35-41): LTI status requires both superposition (additivity plus homogeneity) and invariance to a time shift; squaring is a memorable counterexample because it creates DC, harmonics, and intermodulation products.

Secs. 1.7-1.8 (PDF pp. 41-43): cascaded LTI systems commute, and an LTI system is completely characterized by its impulse response; output is input convolved with that response, while its transform is the system frequency response.
Sec. 2.1 (PDF pp. 52-55): samples of a sinusoid at f0 are indistinguishable from sinusoids at f0+kfs; sampling therefore replicates the continuous spectrum at integer multiples of fs.

Sec. 2.2 (PDF pp. 56-59): a baseband signal limited to B Hz needs fs >= 2B, but the practical acquisition chain still needs an analog lowpass anti-alias filter because any energy above fs/2 folds irreversibly into baseband.

Sec. 2.3 (PDF pp. 59-63): a bandpass signal can often be sampled below twice its highest frequency when its occupied bandwidth is narrow; permissible sample-rate intervals depend on center frequency, bandwidth, and an integer spectral-zone index, while fs must remain at least 2B.
Sec. 2.4 (PDF pp. 63-65): odd spectral folding reverses a band; multiplying samples by (-1)^n shifts the spectrum by fs/2 and can restore its orientation.

Sec. 2.4 (PDF pp. 64-65): bandpass sampling folds out-of-band noise into the recovered band; for the text's zone index m, noise power grows by approximately m+1 and the SNR penalty is 10 log10(m+1) dB (3 dB at m=1).

Sec. 3.1 (PDF pp. 75-85): the N-point DFT measures correlation with complex sinusoids containing integer cycle counts over the N-sample record; bin spacing is Delta f=fs/N, and X(0) is N times the sequence mean.

Sec. 3.2 (PDF pp. 86-87): for real x(n), X(N-m)=X*(m), so an even-length DFT has only N/2+1 independent bins; real-even inputs transform to real-even spectra and real-odd inputs to imaginary-odd spectra.

Sec. 3.4 (PDF p. 88): a bin-centered real sinusoid of peak amplitude A produces magnitude AN/2 in each of its two conjugate bins, a complex sinusoid produces AN in one bin, and DC level D produces DN at bin zero.
Sec. 3.6 (PDF pp. 89-91): circularly shifting the input by k samples multiplies bin m by exp(-j2pi mk/N); magnitude is unchanged and phase acquires a linear ramp.
Sec. 3.7 (PDF pp. 91-92): the IDFT reconstructs the N samples from the bins, reversing the exponent sign and applying the factor 1/N.

Sec. 3.8 (PDF pp. 92-99): a noninteger number of cycles in the record creates an endpoint discontinuity; the finite rectangular observation window makes a tone's spectrum spread according to a sampled sinc/Dirichlet response rather than remain in one bin.
Sec. 3.9 (PDF pp. 99-106): windows reduce leakage sidelobes by tapering endpoints but broaden the main lobe; this is a sensitivity-versus-resolution tradeoff, not a universal improvement.

Secs. 3.9-3.10 (PDF pp. 104-107): the rectangular window's first sidelobe is about -13 dB, and a tone halfway between bins reads only about 0.637 of its true amplitude (roughly 4 dB low in power); Hann/Hanning reduces midpoint scalloping loss to about 1.45 dB while widening the main lobe.

Sec. 3.11 (PDF pp. 107-110): zero padding samples the same DTFT more densely and improves plot/peak interpolation, but it does not resolve tones that the nonzero observation duration cannot separate; acquire about 1/Fres seconds of actual data for resolution Fres.
Sec. 3.12 (PDF pp. 110-113): DFT processing gain for a coherent tone in broadband noise rises by approximately 3 dB whenever N doubles.

Sec. 3.13 (PDF pp. 113-125): a K-sample rectangular pulse has a Dirichlet-kernel spectrum with peak K, first zero near bin N/K, and a main-lobe width of about 2N/K bins, demonstrating the reciprocal time-width/frequency-width relation.

Sec. 3.14 (PDF pp. 125-128): the DTFT is continuous and periodic; an N-point DFT is N uniformly spaced samples of that DTFT and also represents the spectrum of the finite record treated as one period of a periodic sequence.
Sec. 4.1 (PDF pp. 138-140): a radix-2 FFT computes the exact DFT with roughly (N/2)log2(N) complex multiplications instead of N^2; the advantage grows dramatically with N.

Sec. 4.2 (PDF pp. 140-143): choose the nonzero record length from required resolution, pad upward to a convenient FFT length rather than discard valid data, remove mean before applying a window, apply the window before zero padding, and normalize amplitude for real versus complex inputs and window coherent gain.

Sec. 4.3 (PDF pp. 143-150): radix-2 decimation-in-time recursively splits an N-point DFT into even- and odd-index N/2 transforms and joins them with twiddle-factor butterflies; the upper-half outputs reuse lower-half terms with a sign change.
Secs. 4.4-4.5 (PDF pp. 150-154): bit reversal follows from recursive index partitioning; an optimized radix-2 butterfly needs one complex multiplication and two complex additions.

Sec. 4.6 (PDF pp. 154-157): in-place FFTs reduce working storage to about 2N real words but require more intricate addressing, whereas alternating input/output buffers use about 4N real words and simplify routing; twiddles can be precomputed.

Secs. 5.1-5.2 (PDF pp. 168-181): an M-tap FIR output is the convolution sum of current and delayed input samples with M coefficients, and those coefficients are exactly the filter impulse response; the response ends after M output intervals once a finite input ends.

Secs. 5.2-5.3 (PDF pp. 171-195): time-domain convolution corresponds to frequency-domain multiplication, so a filter response is the transform of its impulse response; inverse-transforming an ideal brick-wall response gives an infinite sinc-like impulse response that must be truncated for implementation.

Sec. 5.3 (PDF pp. 181-195): increasing rectangularly truncated FIR length narrows the transition but does not eliminate Gibbs ripple amplitude; a tapered window lowers sidelobe/ripple levels at the cost of a broader transition.

Secs. 5.4-5.5 (PDF pp. 195-197): multiplying lowpass coefficients by a cosine translates the response to bandpass; the fs/4 case yields many zero products, and multiplying coefficient k by (-1)^k translates a lowpass response by fs/2 to make a highpass filter.

Sec. 5.6 (PDF pp. 197-200): Parks-McClellan exchange design finds a Chebyshev-optimal equiripple FIR approximation and normally achieves a narrower transition than a same-length window-designed filter for comparable ripple constraints.

Sec. 5.7 (PDF pp. 200-201): an odd-tap half-band lowpass has symmetry about fs/4 and alternating zero coefficients except its center tap; a 31-tap example needs only 17 multiplications rather than 31.

Sec. 5.8 (PDF pp. 201-206): symmetric or antisymmetric FIR coefficients produce linear phase and constant group delay (N-1)/2 samples; even-tap filters can therefore realize half-sample delay, and linear phase prevents waveform dispersion within the passband.
Sec. 5.9 (PDF pp. 206-216): convolution of finite sequences of lengths P and Q has length P+Q-1; the graphical algorithm reverses one sequence, shifts it, multiplies overlapping samples, and sums.

Sec. 5.10 (PDF pp. 216-224): FIR response can be evaluated directly as a DTFT or with a sufficiently zero-padded FFT of the coefficients; DC gain equals the coefficient sum, phase slope gives group delay, and tap count grows with stopband attenuation and shrinks with transition width.

Secs. 6.1-6.4 (PDF pp. 238-262): an IIR filter adds previous outputs to its difference equation; replacing a one-sample delay by z^-1 turns the block diagram into H(z), and substituting z=exp(jomega) gives its complex frequency response.

Sec. 6.2 (PDF pp. 240-251): on the Laplace s-plane, a stable causal continuous system has every pole in the left half-plane; real part sets exponential growth/decay and imaginary part sets oscillation frequency, while H(jomega) is the frequency response.

Sec. 6.3 (PDF pp. 251-254): the z-plane unit circle is the discrete-frequency contour from -pi to pi radians/sample; a causal IIR filter is stable only if all poles lie inside it, and pole angle sets resonant/oscillation frequency.

Sec. 6.4 (PDF pp. 254-262): a worked second-order IIR has a steeper, lower-sidelobe magnitude response than a five-tap FIR at the same five-multiply workload, but it has nonlinear phase and an asymmetrical, theoretically infinite impulse response.

Sec. 6.5 (PDF pp. 262-267): poles raise response near their unit-circle angles and zeros suppress it; proximity to the unit circle strengthens the effect, a pole or zero on the circle yields infinite gain or attenuation, coincident pairs cancel, and origin poles/zeros do not change frequency response.

Sec. 6.6 (PDF pp. 267-270): Direct Forms I and II and transposed Direct Form II are algebraically equivalent at infinite precision; Direct Form II halves delay storage, while Direct Form I generally resists coefficient/stability error best and transposed Direct Form II behaves better than ordinary Direct Form II in fixed point.

Sec. 6.7 (PDF pp. 270-272): finite word length shifts poles/zeros, permits overflow, and can create zero-input limit cycles through correlated rounding; mitigations include wider words, scaling, saturation arithmetic, dither (with SNR cost), floating point, or an FIR when feedback is unacceptable.

Sec. 6.8 (PDF pp. 272-276): cascaded transfer functions and responses multiply and their impulse responses convolve; parallel transfer functions/responses and impulse responses add. For small linear passband ripples, cascaded ripple is approximately the sum of the section ripples.

Sec. 6.8.2 (PDF pp. 274-276): high-order IIR filters are usually factored into cascaded biquads because low-order sections are easier to scale and less sensitive to coefficient quantization; pair nearby poles and zeros, then order sections by pole distance from the unit circle.

Sec. 6.9 (PDF pp. 276-278): IIR DC gain is the feedforward-coefficient sum divided by one minus the feedback-coefficient sum; scaling feedforward paths can normalize gain without changing response shape, while internal scaling controls overflow/SNR.

Sec. 6.10 (PDF pp. 278-292): impulse invariance samples an analog prototype's impulse response and maps analog poles into the z-plane, but replicated responses alias; it is most suitable for narrow lowpass designs with cutoff far below fs and should not be used for highpass design.

Sec. 6.10 (PDF pp. 280-291): two impulse-invariance workflows are given: inverse-Laplace then z-transform, or partial-fraction decomposition followed by single-pole mappings; including the sample-period factor preserves prototype gain.

Sec. 6.11 (PDF pp. 292-302): the bilinear substitution s=(2/ts)(1-z^-1)/(1+z^-1) maps the left s half-plane inside the unit circle and maps the entire jomega axis one-to-one around the unit circle, avoiding response aliasing.

Sec. 6.11 (PDF pp. 294-301): bilinear frequency mapping is nonlinear: digital frequency approaches pi as analog frequency tends to infinity; prewarp critical analog cutoff frequencies to land them at the desired digital frequencies.

Sec. 6.11.1 (PDF pp. 298-302): in the worked second-order Chebyshev example, bilinear design gives a sharper aliased-free rolloff but uses five multiplications per output versus three for the impulse-invariance implementation; neither method can repair aliasing already present in sampled input data.

Sec. 6.12 (PDF pp. 302-303): optimized IIR design iteratively adjusts numerator and denominator coefficients to minimize a specified response error and is the practical default for arbitrary shapes and often for standard filters as well.

Sec. 6.13 (PDF pp. 303-305): FIR is required for exact linear phase, while IIR often meets magnitude requirements with fewer multipliers and can emulate analog prototypes; on a real DSP, benchmark both because FIR MAC loops can outperform multiply-count intuition.
pedagogy: The shard is an engineer-facing, intuition-first treatment that introduces each abstraction through sampled plots, small block diagrams, numerical counterexamples, and implementation consequences before consolidating it algebraically. Proofs are mostly short derivations by substitution or inspection; formal transform machinery is deliberately motivated through correlation, impulse-response, and pole/zero pictures rather than measure-theoretic arguments. The narrative repeatedly flags sign conventions, scaling traps, aliasing, coefficient precision, and misleading visual interpretations, making it strong as a practical companion to a more theorem-heavy course. Worked examples are unusually concrete: hand DFTs, window comparisons, an 8-point radix-2 FFT, a moving-average FIR, window/equiripple/half-band FIR design, a complete z-plane IIR analysis, and parallel impulse-invariance and bilinear Chebyshev designs. End-of-chapter exercise volume is substantial (24, 22, 25, 18, 29, and 50 problems respectively) and mixes conceptual explanations, sketches, hand calculations, block-diagram conversions, parameter design, and software plots; many problems have several parts and are suitable for labs. Prerequisites are algebra, trigonometry, complex numbers, and basic calculus; Laplace and z transforms are introduced sufficiently for the examples, though a learner without systems background will benefit from supplementary transform practice. The best teaching reuse is a cycle of predict from a diagram, calculate a small example, inspect a spectrum or pole plot, then test the implementation pitfall.

gems: Sec. 1.1 (PDF p. 27): the insistence that there is literally no defined signal between plotted samples is a small but powerful correction to the common habit of mentally connecting the dots.
Sec. 1.8 (PDF pp. 42-43): a four-point moving average is introduced by striking the system with a unit impulse, then reading both the coefficient sequence and lowpass behavior from the response.
Sec. 2.1 (PDF pp. 52-55): the 7 kHz versus 1 kHz alias produced at a 6 kHz sample rate makes frequency ambiguity immediately audible/visual rather than merely algebraic.
Sec. 2.3 (PDF pp. 59-63): a band centered near 20 MHz with only 5 MHz bandwidth can occupy valid sampling intervals around 11.25-11.67 MHz instead of forcing a conventional rate above 45 MHz.
Sec. 2.4 (PDF pp. 63-65): the 'shark's teeth' view of successive spectral zones makes alternating normal/inverted aliases memorable, and (-1)^n becomes a one-multiply-per-sample repair.
Sec. 3.1 (PDF pp. 75-85): the hand-worked 8-point DFT of 1 kHz and 2 kHz sinusoids sampled at 8 kHz is compact enough for learners to verify every real and imaginary contribution.

Secs. 3.8-3.9 (PDF pp. 92-106): keeping the record length fixed while changing a tone from 3.0 to 3.4 cycles, then adding a weak second tone and windowing, provides a complete leakage-to-detection narrative.
Sec. 3.11 (PDF pp. 107-110): padding the same 16 samples to successively larger transforms visually separates 'more dots on the same curve' from genuine resolving power.
Sec. 3.12 (PDF pp. 110-113): one repeated tone-in-noise example at three N values turns the abstract 3 dB-per-doubling processing gain into an obvious measurement advantage.
Sec. 4.1 (PDF pp. 138-140): the scale comparison is vivid: a 2,097,152-point FFT is framed as seconds of work while the direct DFT would require weeks on the same basis.
Sec. 4.2 (PDF pp. 140-143): the practical ordering rule 'subtract the mean, window the acquired samples, then append zeros' prevents several common spectral-analysis mistakes in one line of workflow.
Secs. 5.1-5.2 (PDF pp. 168-181): a five-minute moving average of bridge traffic is an unusually accessible bridge from an everyday table to convolution, impulse response, and lowpass filtering.

Sec. 5.6 (PDF pp. 197-200): the historical aside about Parks and McClellan's exchange-method paper being rejected is paired with the Beatles/Decca rejection, making algorithmic novelty and peer-review fallibility memorable.
Sec. 5.7 (PDF pp. 200-201): the 31-tap half-band example collapses to 17 multiplies because of alternating zeros and symmetry, a strong structure-before-optimization lesson.
Sec. 5.8 (PDF pp. 201-206): the group-delay discussion ties a straight phase line directly to preserving a signal's component alignment instead of treating linear phase as a cosmetic plot property.

Sec. 6.4.2 (PDF pp. 258-262): the mnemonic 'z-domain produces less pain' accompanies a real modeling advantage: writing equations from z^-1 block notation usually introduces fewer intermediate unknowns.
Sec. 6.6.1 (PDF pp. 267-269): Lyons sharply distinguishes recursive/nonrecursive as implementation structure from IIR/FIR as impulse-response duration, correcting a widespread terminology shortcut.

Sec. 6.7 (PDF pp. 270-272): an integer-rounded, zero-input second-order filter that rings forever is a laboratory-ready demonstration that mathematical stability does not guarantee a quiet fixed-point implementation.
Sec. 6.8.2 (PDF pp. 274-276): 'biquad' is motivated both by the two quadratic polynomials and, humorously, because the word sounds cool; the levity helps anchor a central implementation unit.
Sec. 6.10 (PDF pp. 288-292): the warning that any spectrum or filter response nonzero at +fs/2 should trigger immediate aliasing suspicion is a concise review heuristic.

Sec. 6.13 (PDF pp. 303-305): the recommendation to code and time both candidates when choosing IIR versus FIR exposes why multiplier counts alone can mislead on DSP hardware with zero-overhead MAC loops.
chapter_map: Front matter (PDF pp. 1-25): establishes the book's practical-engineer audience, notation, learning posture, and detailed route through the assigned chapters.

Chapter 1, Discrete Sequences and Systems (PDF pp. 26-51): builds the sampled-sequence vocabulary, block-diagram primitives, LTI tests, impulse response, convolution, and frequency response; use as the conceptual entry module.

Chapter 2, Periodic Sampling (PDF pp. 52-73): develops aliasing from sinusoidal ambiguity through lowpass and bandpass sampling, spectral inversion, and noise folding; use before any acquisition or resampling lab.

Chapter 3, The Discrete Fourier Transform (PDF pp. 74-137): interprets every DFT term, then develops symmetry, scaling, shifts, leakage, windows, scalloping, resolution, zero padding, processing gain, rectangular transforms, and DTFT context; this is the core spectral-analysis module.

Chapter 4, The Fast Fourier Transform (PDF pp. 138-166): moves from DFT cost to radix-2 factorization, bit reversal, butterflies, and memory architectures while retaining practical measurement advice; pair with an 8-point hand trace and code benchmark.

Chapter 5, Finite Impulse Response Filters (PDF pp. 167-236): introduces convolutional filtering, develops window and Parks-McClellan design, modulation, half-band efficiency, linear phase/group delay, generic convolution, and response analysis; use as the primary FIR design-and-implementation module.

Chapter 6, Infinite Impulse Response Filters (PDF pp. 237-327): develops Laplace/z-plane intuition, poles/zeros, structures, fixed-point failure modes, cascaded biquads, scaling, impulse-invariance, bilinear, and optimized design, ending with an evidence-based FIR/IIR choice; use as a combined IIR theory, implementation, and design module.
